title: Resistance and Return
subtitle: Three years of guerrilla war, and what the return cost.
objectives: Explain the return and the Leyte landing
Describe the Battle of Manila and its cost
Explain the state of the country in 1945

cards.title: Occupied is not the same as conquered
cards.text: For three years the fighting never fully stopped. It just moved into the hills and into the towns.

cards.title: A war fought in pieces
cards.text: Resistance groups operated across the islands, with no single command.
points: **Former soldiers, farmers, students and teachers.**
**They gathered intelligence**, ambushed patrols and kept maps.
**Radios kept some in contact** with Allied forces.
**Reprisals against villages** were the cost of every raid.

question.text: Why did guerrilla raids carry a heavy cost for civilians?
options: Occupying forces took reprisals against villages
question.explain: Collective punishment of nearby communities was a standard response.

cards.title: Leyte, October 1944
cards.text: The Allied return began in the central islands, not in Luzon.
points: **MacArthur landed at Leyte** in October 1944.
**He had promised 'I shall return'** in 1942.
**Osmeña, now President, came with him.**
**The campaign north** took months more.

cards.title: Why Leyte and not Manila
cards.text: You take the place that gives you airfields, not the place with the famous name.
points: **Airfields first**, then everything else becomes possible.
**Leyte Gulf** could land men and supplies.
**Air cover from there** reached Luzon.
**The same logic** that lost the islands in 1941 won them back.

cards.title: The cost of taking the city back
cards.text: The battle for Manila in February 1945 was among the most destructive of the war.
points: **About a month of street fighting.**
**Roughly 100,000 civilians died.**
**The old walled city, Intramuros, was largely destroyed.**
**Manila was one of the most damaged capitals** of the entire war.

question.text: Manila was recaptured with little damage because it had been an open city in 1941.
question.explain: The 1941 declaration did not apply in 1945. The battle destroyed much of the city and killed around 100,000 civilians.

cards.title: What a destroyed country actually means
cards.text: Independence arrived in 1946 to a place that had to be rebuilt first.
points: **Bridges, ports and railways** were wrecked.
**Schools and hospitals** gone or occupied.
**Farms had been stripped**, so food was short.
**A new country** starting from less than nothing.

question.text: Roughly how many civilians died in the Battle of Manila?
question.explain: Around 100,000, in about a month of street fighting.

cards.title: 'I shall return' is remembered because he did
cards.text: Promises in war are usually forgotten. This one was repeated until it became a fact.
points: **He said it in 1942**, leaving for Australia.
**He landed at Leyte in October 1944.**
**The phrase was deliberate**, and he refused to change it.
**Osmeña walked ashore with him**, which is less often remembered.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 4 Social Studies, the second occupation week, covering resistance and liberation. The guerrilla section is built around the reprisal problem rather than around heroism, because that is the honest shape of the choice: every raid was also a decision about a nearby village. Leyte is explained by the same air-power logic that lost the islands in 1941, which ties the two weeks together causally. The Battle of Manila is given its real figure, about 100,000 civilian dead, and the week closes on the condition of the country in 1946 so that the challenges of independence in weeks 5 and 6 follow from something concrete.
discussion: Why was every guerrilla raid also a decision about civilians?
Why land at Leyte rather than Manila?
extension: Find out whether your province had a named guerrilla unit.
Look at photographs of Intramuros before and after 1945.
misconceptions: That Manila was spared because of 1941.
That independence began from a normal starting point.
